newsitem.title: USA: Powerless New Englanders look beyond snow to spring.
newsitem.headline: Powerless New Englanders look beyond snow to spring.

text.p: Massachusetts remained under a state of emergency Wednesday with thousands of residents still without power and frustrated travelers stranded at Boston's Logan International Airport, as temperatures climbed into the 50s under a clear, blue sky.

One day after the record-breaking storm struck, burying the region in up to three feet of snow, area hospitals began reporting a number of weather-related injuries including back sprains and hand injuries from snowblowers.
Massachusetts General Hospital reported at least three people suffered head injuries after being struck by huge blocks of the melting heavy, snow plummeting from buildings.

Meanwhile, service was slowly being restored throughout the region. Boston Edison, which had had 60,000 outages at the height of the storm, reported 16,000 customers were still without power. Massachusetts Electric, a subsidiary of the New England Electric Systems, had up to 117,000 customers without power Tuesday, but by Wednesday afternoon had restored service to all but 9,900.
Commonwealth Electric, a subsidiary of Commonwealth Energy Systems, reported that it still had 29,000 customers, mostly on Cape Cod and Martha's Vineyard, without power.

"There will not be a return to full service probably until Friday," Commonwealth Electric spokesman Peter Dimond said, despite hundreds of crews that were called in from as far away as Maryland and Canada.

Logan airport was operating with only one runway but hoped to have full service restored by the end of the day Wednesday. Stranded passengers, some of whom had been huddled in airport terminals since Monday night, were busy rebooking flights and airport officials estimated that some of them would not be out before Friday.
While highways and interstates in the region were clear, many streets and secondary roads remained impassable, state officials said.
In Boston, Mayor Thomas Menino said that despite having more than 400 ploughs out, many parts of the city remained buried in the 25.4 inches of snow that fell Tuesday.
"Snowplows just can't this heavy, wet snow. It really takes backhoes and dump trucks," he said.
The sheer volume impressed visitors to the region. Paul Parker of Leeds, England, who landed in New York and drove to western Massachusetts Monday night, was awed by the storm.
"I thought it was amazing," Parker said, wearing shorts as he shoveled a friend's driveway. "We get two-to-three inches of snow in England. Never the volume of this."
Most schools in Massachusetts and in parts of Connecticut and Rhode Island were closed for a second day because of the blizzard.
"It is the snowiest April on record for Boston and Massachusetts," National Weather Service forecaster William Babcock said. The previous record was 13.3 inches in 1982.

The storm's after effects continued to plague parts of the region. Strong winds, with gusts over 35 mph, were forecast for coastal New England and ocean wave heights were expected to taper down to 10-to-20 feet.
